facts_from_discussion: The payments Dr. Ibrahim made to Ms. Edington were made in cash (by check).

Respondent agrees that the payments were received by Ms. Edington under a divorce or separation instrument and that Dr. Ibrahim and Ms. Edington were not members of the same household when the payments were made.
The agreement, the amended agreement, and the judgment each contain statements that neither Dr. Ibrahim nor Ms. Edington would pay maintenance to (or receive maintenance from) the other.
Under Missouri law since 1973, courts award 'maintenance' rather than 'alimony'; the court treats the two terms as synonymous for federal income tax purposes.
The agreement, the amended agreement, and the judgment contain no express provision terminating the payments upon Ms. Edington's death.

Missouri law (Mo. Rev. Stat. 452.370(3)) provides that, unless otherwise agreed in writing or expressly provided in the judgment, the obligation to pay future statutory maintenance terminates upon the death of either party or the remarriage of the recipient.
No Missouri state court found that Ms. Edington was eligible for maintenance under Missouri law.

Ms. Edington was continuously employed as a nurse during and after the marriage, was able to rent and later purchase a home during the separation, and (per Dr. Ibrahim's own testimony) was able to support herself financially during and after the divorce.
The court found that Dr. Ibrahim did not show that the payments were made because of an obligation to pay future statutory maintenance under Missouri law.
$1,200 of the payments was paid during 2016, not during 2017.

The initial determination to impose the accuracy-related penalty was made by Mrs. Bowden on May 8, 2019; the 30-day letter of May 10, 2019 was the first communication of the penalty; her immediate supervisor approved the penalty in writing on May 8, 2019, before the 30-day letter.

The court found that Dr. Ibrahim did not show reasonable cause or good faith: he claimed the deduction although the agreement, amended agreement, and judgment explicitly stated that neither party was entitled to maintenance.
Dr. Ibrahim did not identify authorities supporting his return position (substantial authority claim) nor address contrary authorities.
